name: Sprites
oneLiner: Persistent Fly.io microVMs that suspend after about 30 seconds idle and bill measured CPU and memory.
whatItIs: Sprites are persistent Linux environments on Fly.io for agents, development and user-submitted code. Each is a dedicated microVM with a whole filesystem that survives between sessions.
The design assumes a computer that sleeps: a short idle window suspends it with memory frozen, and a longer idle period stops it and drops memory, keeping the disk.
whoFor: Developers who want a long-lived Linux computer for an agent, with automatic sleep and usage-based billing rather than a reserved size.
isolation: Dedicated microVM with hardware-level isolation. Root is available and Docker is reported to work, but Sprites do not run systemd: a built-in service manager starts services on wake.
sizes: One fixed shape: 8 vCPUs and 100 GB of storage, with memory assigned and autoscaled per Sprite. No published region selection, GPU or ARM option.

billing.model: Measured usage, with optional monthly plans that bundle allowances.
billing.meter: Actual CPU at $0.0385 per CPU-hour and actual memory at $0.021875 per GB-hour while awake; hot storage at $0.000683 per GB-hour and cold storage at $0.000027 per GB-hour.
billing.stopped: No compute charge in warm or cold state, but cold storage is billed for as long as data is kept.
billing.planFee: The pricing page says there are no plans; the product FAQ describes plans including Hero at $100 a month. Both are current.
billing.minimum: No published minimum. A one-time $30 trial credit per user and per organisation, which cannot pay a subscription fee.

facts.label: Legal entity
facts.value: Fly.io, Inc., a Delaware corporation. Sprites is a product on Fly's platform, not a separate company.

source.quote: The contracting party for all Fly.io services is Fly.io, Inc.

facts.label: Leadership
facts.value: Scott Johnston is CEO; founder Kurt Mackey moved to an advisory role and remains on the board.

source.quote: Fly.io also announced that Scott Johnston has joined as CEO and a member of the board.

facts.label: History and funding
facts.value: Fly has run the platform since 2017 and launched Sprites on 9 January 2026. A $25M Series D in July 2026, co-led by Dell Technologies Capital and Intel Capital.

source.quote: $25 million in Series D funding co-led by Dell Technologies Capital and Intel Capital, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, EQT, Geodesic, and YC.

facts.label: Status and SLA
facts.value: Sprites is a component on Fly's status page with no numeric uptime figure. Fly's 99.9% SLA is Enterprise-only and credits must be claimed.

source.quote: will apply to the Services for Customers with an Enterprise plan during the applicable Subscription Term

facts.label: Certification
facts.value: SOC 2 Type 2 covers the Fly platform and does not name Sprites; the report and BAA sit behind a $99-a-month compliance package.

source.quote: The report describes the Fly.io platform; it does not name individual products such as Sprites, which run on the platform it covers

facts.label: Headcount
facts.value: Not published. Fly lists team members but no headcount figure.

well: An agent that pauses constantly: a warm pause after about 30 seconds resumes in 100–500 ms.
A long-lived filesystem with no volume to manage, capped at 100 GB and billed on bytes written.
Secrets that never reach the Sprite, through connectors and a gateway.
badly: systemd: Sprites do not run it, and services start through a built-in manager on wake.
A live fork or create-from-checkpoint: neither is documented.
A client-facing link: the URL is private to the organisation and needs an org token.

usability.dashboard: A dashboard exists for connector setup and a Gateway Playground that can fire a request without code.
usability.withoutCode: Limited. The documented start path installs a CLI and opens a console; the no-code surface is connector testing, not running an agent.
usability.signup: Uses a Fly.io account. Card requirement, waitlist and trial duration are not published.
usability.docs: Fly documentation covers lifecycle, checkpoints, networking and connectors. Support is community on lower plans and varies by plan.
tripsUp: Warm and cold are different states, and the transition is not user-selected.
Open TCP connections do not survive a pause, warm or cold.
Checkpoints are filesystem snapshots, not memory snapshots.
Cold storage bills while the Sprite is kept.

caveats.issue: The pricing page and product FAQ disagree on plans
caveats.detail: Pricing says there are no plans and nothing charged per Sprite; the FAQ describes plans including Hero at $100 a month with CPU, RAM and storage allowances.

evidence.quote: No plans and no tiers, and nothing charged per Sprite.
Plans bundle an allowance of CPU-hours, RAM GB-hours, and storage GB, not unlimited usage.

caveats.detail: The idle window before warm suspension is about 30 seconds; how long before a Sprite drops to cold is not stated.

caveats.issue: Storage charges while idle are ambiguous
caveats.detail: The FAQ says warm and cold are not billed, while the pricing page bills cold storage for as long as data is kept.

evidence.quote: Sprites have three states: running (billed), warm (not billed), and cold (not billed).
Cold Bills for as long as you keep it

caveats.issue: No fork or create-from-checkpoint is documented
caveats.detail: Checkpoints restore in place and overwrite current files; a live fork or clone is not established.

caveats.issue: Region selection and architecture are unpublished
caveats.detail: No provider-confirmed region list, GPU option or CPU architecture statement was found.

strengths: The whole filesystem persists between sessions, not one mounted folder.
Warm suspension keeps processes and resumes in 100–500 ms.
Copy-on-write checkpoints that do not interrupt work.
Connectors keep credentials in the gateway, not the guest.
